title: Needing some advice on how to proceed as a game dev

posts.author: Prescott
posts.body:
For context, I am nearly 30 years old and I've been using various versions of RPG Maker since I was 10. I made many small games, most of which never came to fruition, but I've learned an immense amount about the way the engines work over this period of time. My passion project, God's Disdain, was released earlier this year in March after I had worked on it for 10 years, overcoming a lot of struggles with motivation and other things going on in my life. So far, the game has not seen the reception I would have hoped it would, which is certainly a mix of several factors but I would be lying if I said it wasn't disappointing.
Back in 2018, I began writing and making design documents for a horror game that I wanted to make. Ideally, I would love for this game to be a 3D game in a similar vein to the original Silent Hill. I had a few friends who were willing to start learning Unreal Engine and modeling/texturing, but unfortunately they fell off pretty quickly. After that happened, I put the game on the backburner and refocused on God's Disdain.
After releasing God's Disdain, I took a bit of a break but then started looking for an engine that could achieve something as close to my vision for this horror game. I had already done this once before back in 2018 and had found that Unreal Engine was going to be the best, but since then some new options have made themselves known to me.
The first I experimented with was RPG Developer Bakin, but it was really clunky and had some issues on my system and I just didn't vibe with the engine at all.
The second was RPG Architect, since it was familiar to RPG Maker but did have 3D capability and was actually built for it. However, it is extremely similar to MV/MZ 3D which is a workflow I'm just not very fond of. If you could develop the maps in a 3D space and visualize them in real time I think I would be much more interested in that route. I think its similarity to RPG Maker is also weirdly a detriment for me, because it feels just similar enough that it is frustrating when something doesn't work in exactly the same way. It has an absurd amount of potential for making your game, but again... it just wasn't something I vibe with.
The third, and what I'm currently on, is RPG In A Box. It's been in development for years, and uses voxels for 3D modeling. It has a 3D map editor, the UI is actually really good, and you can create all of your voxel models within the engine itself. It has its own easy to learn coding language and projects can be exported to Godot since the engine was created with it in the first place. I like the engine a lot, actually. On top of this, it has an announced update for the future that is going to include simple polygon model editing and true gridless movement (right now it only exists for the player, not any other entities). I do believe that this engine would be the engine I could make my ideal version of this horror game in, but there is one issue.
Time. Learning a new engine from the ground up in a way that I can develop every aspect of the game that I have wanted to include is going to take a lot of time. When I compare how much time I've spent with RPG Maker to this, it feels like I would be trying to climb a mountain in a rowboat. I feel pretty confident I can make everything I wanted for this game with RPG Maker except for the exact 3D style I had envisioned. I need something like RPG In A Box for that.
If this were the only thing I wanted to do with my life for the next ten years, then maybe it would be justifiable. If I had a pretty solid group of people who were all in on this with me, helping with the modeling and texturing and perhaps even some coding, it would make it a lot easier to proceed as well.
The issue is that I just have so many other things I want to make, and I don't want another situation to happen like it did with God's Disdain. The vast majority of the team who worked on various aspects the game moved on with their lives long before the game came out, and even from them I heard very little fanfare. All of the hype I had built up for the game through word of mouth had completely died off as people sort of realized that this wasn't coming out, and by the time it did they had also moved on to other things. I don't know of anyone who has even beaten the thing because something else has come up that takes precedent, like other releases they are more interested in. I know that the game itself probably isn't some god-tier thing either and it has plenty of issues and perhaps it just really isn't compelling enough, but there was a period where pretty much everyone I knew in real life was dying to play it and I just missed that opportunity to capitalize because it was just taking so long.
On top of this horror game, I also have plans for two sequels to God's Disdain, another horror game, and a space drama. I want to make these games before I die lol. That's hyperbole, but I think you can get what I'm saying. It's just really hard for me to justify leaning all in to a new engine with a much, much smaller community, even though I know I could eventually create what I really want to, when I can get most of the way there with shirking just 1 (albeit major) feature and get the game done in half the time or less with RPG Maker. Then there's the issue that I actually would prefer that the God's Disdain sequels are done in 2D and it makes it even harder to justify.
I've thought about maybe putting together a team, finding some likeminded individuals who want to push for an awesome 3D horror experience, but my experience with teams has just been extremely fleeting. The only way I could get so many people to work on God's Disdain is because they were doing one specific task over the course of a few months, max. Some people didn't completely finish their work, and I ended up having to finish it instead or get somebody else to chip in real quick. This horror game would be a much larger endeavor than those few months, which would require a lot of teamwork and cooperation that I just haven't ever experienced. That's another fear I have with wasting time... that I would get so far into a project while heavily relying on others and then it would just crumble.
As I post this though, and as I deliberate, I am also wasting time. I am wasting time by not deciding on something. Analysis paralysis, they call it. That's why I'm turning this over to other people and asking for some advice on how to proceed. You guys may be biased because this is an RPG Maker forum, of course, but you are also all game developers and pretty sensible, all things considered.
Going to RPG In A Box would be fully (or near fully) realizing the ideal image of the game I have in my head, and potentially getting more people interested as the game wouldn't be 2D and wouldn't be confined to the "RPG Maker Horror" niche. It would just take a lot longer than I would like, and although this is a fault of my own it would be harder to work up the motivation to keep chipping away at something like that.
Staying with RPG Maker would be making a concession (which I've become viscerally aware of with game development when trying to finish something) on the 3D aspect, but with the knowledge that I will be able to make everything else fit together in a much faster time period and without relying so much on other people. It's a safer option, and it allows me to make more of what I want to make faster, but that could also theoretically be to the game's detriment itself.
You may notice that my prioritization of time is pretty clear from my choice of what engines I have decided to pursue as well. Obviously, I could make a game 10x more visually interesting and technologically advanced and whatever with something like Unreal or Unity than RPG Architect, RPG Developer Bakin, or RPG In A Box, but these were all engines that I felt would allow me to create things I want to create within a reasonable timeframe. At the end of the day, I am still just a hobbyist.
What are you guys thoughts on this? Do you have any experience with any of this you could share that might help me choose what I should do? Any other just general advice? Sorry to put you through the inconvenience of reading this but I felt like this was a pretty good place to ask.

posts.body: Sounds like midlife crisis. On another note, have you considered just commissioning a plugin to get the 3d look you're looking for? Or having someone edit the existing 3d plugins to work how you want? Seems to me like the most sensible option if you don't have that time to learn a new engine.

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
I mean that's exactly what you do with plugins... You can write code to do virtually anything. I've not played Silent Hill, as I'm no Horror fan, but from the looks of it, it's your average tank controls character and fixed per-room-camera angles resident evil had. To be honest I'm almost sure you can do that with the regular MV3D. Maybe with some code adjustments.
The only real hurdle I see is getting those 3d models to work. I know MV3D can convert sprites into 3d models, but I haven't used it myself to really know how that works and if it can be used for more complex things than rtp sprites.
On the other hand, maybe learning unreal isn't so bad. You can totally make 2d games in that as well for your other projects and as you said, it may suit your needs for this horror game way better.
Getting a team together is most likely not a realistic option unless you pay them a wage. Nobody is ever going to care about your game as much as you do, and all the people here have their own games to work on too. So I guess just take good care of your health so you can live up to 150 and make those games!

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Here's advice from a Zombie who is much older than you and who is realizing more and more that he has far fewer years in front of him than behind him.
Focus on the journey and not the destination.
If you enjoy making games and you think you would enjoy learning a new engine and new skills, then it is time well spent. You can look back later with fond memories of what you did, what you learned, and the journey itself.
But if you are over focused on the destination and the anticipated end result, then I honestly think that most of the time, you will end up disappointed. In my experience, things very rarely end up coming out exactly as we initially envisioned them or how we dreamed about. Especially with something that takes years to achieve.
This is also why some people experience a significant "let down" when they finally achieve such a goal. Because the reality of achieving it wasn't anywhere near as spectacular and momentous as they thought it would be.
As an example, it took me well over 20 years to final achieve black belt rank in a martial arts style. For many different reasons. But when it finally happened, I won't say it was a disappointment, but I will say it wasn't anywhere near as momentous as I thought it would be.
But, I look back at the journey and I wouldn't change any of it.
Just my opinion, but you can waste a lot of time and experience a lot of anxiety if you evaluate all your future activities comparing available time versus total time potentially left versus what you hope to gain or experience from said future activity.
I have learned not to think about whether or not I have enough time to actually finish or achieve something that I'm thinking about pursuing, learning, or trying. I now focus more on whether or not I'm going to enjoy doing it.
If so, then I forge ahead. If not, then I look for something else to catch my interest.
Anyway, good luck and remember to enjoy what you do!

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
ZombieKidzRule said:
This is also why some people experience a significant "let down" when they finally achieve such a goal. Because the reality of achieving it wasn't anywhere near as spectacular and momentous as they thought it would be.
Click to expand...
Realistically most games take the devs years to make only for the players to play it for a few hours/days, drop it a few hours in, then move on to the next game.
I've personally taken inspiration from UFO 50 as a lesson in keeping scope manageable while still delivering quality so I can have a hope of actually finishing game. I have like four half finished projects.
I've also been working a lot more in Gdevelop rather than RPG Maker for its flexibility in creating any genre of game and then being able to reuse code between games. It also gets updates and improvements far more often than RPG Maker. RPG Maker is great for making turn-based, grid-based RPGs, it's hyperspecialized for it, but unless that's all you want to make general purpose engines are better.
OP, I recommend you keep each game's scope/ambition smaller. This will make it less overwhelming and also keep your personal investment in time and energy in check so you don't burn out or feel as disappointed if a project has weak reception (i.e. fail fast). Sometimes you need to keep throwing ideas at a wall to see what sticks. Also you can always reuse code or assets in another game so even if the game flops it's not a total loss.

Click to expand...
I'm older than you and can code just fine. I still went with GDevelop, a no code engine, because it was easy to pick up from RPG Maker (its event pages work a lot like parallel common events and it uses javascript if you do want to code), it's growing fast and updates weekly, and I think it has a promising future. It also has a built in 3D editor they are pushing more updates to lately. I find I have to code a lot less in GD than RPG Maker to do what I want. In RPG Maker I'm constantly editing code in plugin files or writing full blocks of script in the script box.
That said, if you want to make an RPG, RPG Maker has more of the RPG systems (shop, equipment, battle system, etc) prebuilt for you, saving you time. You could do it GD or another engine, but it would require designing and building it from scratch (or a more limited template). The flip side is you have far more control over their design and customization since well, you built it.
The big engines (Unity, Unreal and Godot) are obviously more powerful (especially for 3D) but for smaller scope games you want to churn out fast with no coding something like GD's just fine.

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
No problem. Ultimately a game engine is just a tool. Some are specialized and very good at their niche, others are generalized Swiss army knives that can do a lot of jobs decently but not as fast at a specialized application.
It's fine to have more than one tool in your box.

posts.author: rpgLord69
posts.body:
I think the era of getting people to play your hobby game was left in 2015 (if you're talking more than a few thousand players over the course of years or getting some kind of continued feedback or excitement). Unless you make a game like Fear and Hunger, or something like Seed of Nostalgia where every aspect is polished and you also manage good gameplay (for the genre).
Nowadays it's like a hobbyist band complaining that people don't show up to their concert. Too saturated. You might need to do constant marketing and network with other RM/other devs (outside of here) who'll share your stuff on social media to get any kind of reach.
So if you have any expectations, you'll probably get depressed LOL. Maybe a part why people don't finish their projects or take so long to finish them. I think 99% people will be disappointed here. Though if people close to your irl lost interest, I get that hurts.
So whether you switch to a new engine or continue with RPG Maker, the enjoyment will mostly have to come from devving itself, learning new stuff or interacting with other devs / showing your progress to an audience (most of whom won't play your game but some might engage with your pics etc). Or else you're probably just building another disappointment.

There's also the "fail fast, fail often" aspect to it.

Oh, believe me, I know all about the music stuff! I've been doing creative things like that for as long as I can remember and my parents barely even listened to it lol. I'm not trying to trauma dump or anything, but it does make for an interesting point of comparison because with stuff like that and a lot of other things I've done, there was lackluster support from the start. With God's Disdain, I had an absurd amount of initial support, to the point where I wouldn't have been able to make the game without it, and then it all kind of vanished by the end and that was the more disappointing part to me than just seeing low engagement. Does that make sense?
It's like the common advice I've seen that you shouldn't start advertising your game until 1-2 years before its release because you'll lose interest after that point. People will think it is never coming out and then they'll check out entirely. That's the kind of thing I want to avoid, and I think being able to make a game faster will help with that at the very least.
At the same time, I do still want to create the things I want to create instead of making really small projects. Those are fun and I'll still continue doing those when I get the urge of course. During the development of God's Disdain I made four other smaller ones that took anywhere from a week to a few months to make. Helped keep things fresh for sure. I just get the most pleasure in game dev making those big projects I think, rather than making the little short stuff. This is more a question of how best to manage my time, even though it's probably really convoluted because I have a bad habit of rambling haha.
I am thinking what I'll probably do is continue to work with RPG In A Box for fun when I'm feeling like it, but develop this horror game I have in RPG Maker over the next few years. I think talking about it more and more with people online and offline has made me realize that, just like with any other game development ideal, it doesn't necessarily need to be 3D as long as I'm still going to enjoy the end product and enjoy the journey.

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
Prescott said:
At the same time, I do still want to create the things I want to create instead of making really small projects.
Click to expand...
The idea is you start small (e.g. "rapid prototyping") to test the validity and market response then expand, pivot, or scrap the idea based on feedback. If you have a hit, build on the idea, if it's a miss, then it's back to the drawing board. Don't take the results personally. Massive companies with teams of professional marketers and analysts produce flops all the time.
Your game may have had weak reception but at least you didn't spend years of dev teams' time and hundreds of millions on it like Concord or Unknown 9.
